transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Uh, well, what brings me in is... I just feel like I’ve got this motor humming under my skin whenever I’m supposed to sit still. You know, like during staff meetings at work—I clean office buildings—or during church event briefings. I just end up shifting in my chair, standing up, or finding some excuse to move around. 

Like last Sunday, they were going over the volunteer schedule for the food drive, and I just had to get up and check the thermostat. Speaking of thermostats, the ones in those old church halls are completely shot. I told the pastor, I said, "You can't expect a boiler from 1985 to keep up with these temperature swings." I mean, I see it all the time at my day job. People are always messing with the dials in the offices. And you wouldn't believe what they flush down the toilets in those corporate buildings, either. Just last Tuesday I spent two hours unclogging a drain on the fourth floor because someone dropped a whole... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right. Yeah, so sitting still in those meetings. I just can't do it, I always have to be up and moving.

Have you noticed these periods where you feel like you have a 'motor' inside you happen in distinct episodes lasting days or weeks, with other times where you feel completely back to your normal self?

Episodes? Uh, no, not really. It’s not like it comes and goes for a week and then stops. It’s just... every day. I don't really know what a 'normal self' without it would even look like, honestly. My wife says I’ve been like this since we met at the community college. 

Actually, speaking of that, I originally went there to get my associate's in HVAC repair. It’s funny how life works out, 'cause I ended up just doing general building maintenance and cleaning instead. The HVAC guys make a killing, but man, they have to crawl into these tiny, dusty ducts all day. I knew a guy, Jimmy, who actually got stuck in a ventilation shaft over at the old strip mall. Took the fire department three hours to get him out. They had to use industrial dish soap or something to slide him loose. He was furious, and he smelled like lemon fresh Joy for a month. 

But, uh... wait. What were we talking about? Oh, right, the motor feeling. Yeah, no, it's just an everyday thing for me, not like an episode or anything.
Do you find yourself feeling constantly worried or anxious about a wide range of different things in your life, such as your job performance, your finances, or your health?

Anxious? Worried? No, not really. I mean, I don't sit around stressing about my health or my bank account or anything like that. I just do my job, you know? Though, speaking of my job, they did just switch our cleaning supplier at work, and let me tell you, this new floor wax is garbage. It leaves these streaks down the hallway, especially when the afternoon sun hits the linoleum on the third floor. I told my supervisor, I said, "You're saving pennies but you're making me do the job twice." 

And it's not just the wax, it's the paper towels too. They got these cheap, thin ones now that just dissolve in your hands the second they touch water. I remember back in '98, we used to get these heavy-duty industrial rolls. You could practically dry a whole car with one sheet. My buddy Dave used to take a roll home every month for his garage. He was rebuilding a '69 Mustang. Beautiful car. Cherry red. He ended up selling it to pay for his kid's college, which is a shame, really, because... 

Wait, sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, worrying. No, I don't really worry about stuff constantly. I just get antsy, you know?
Looking back at your time in school as a child, before you were an adult, did you struggle with sitting still or paying attention in class back then too?

Oh, yeah, absolutely. I was always in trouble back in grade school. I remember I'd always be popping out of my seat, talking over the teacher, just rushing ahead to do whatever before they even finished giving the directions. My mother used to say I acted like I was wound too tight, even back then. 

She used to say the same thing about my Uncle Charlie, actually. He was a piece of work. He used to fix up old radios in his garage—those big, wooden cabinet ones from the 1940s. He had this whole system for organizing the vacuum tubes, little glass things everywhere. I remember one time he let me help him solder a wire, and I accidentally dropped the iron on his favorite work stool. Burned a hole right through the vinyl padding. He didn't even get mad, just patched it up with some silver duct tape. That tape stayed on there for twenty years. You know, duct tape really isn't good for ducts, ironically. The heat makes the adhesive dry out and peel off. That's why we use the aluminum foil tape at work. It's way more expensive, but... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, school. Yeah, I couldn't sit still or wait my turn back then either. It's always been like this.
Besides having trouble sitting still, do you often find that you have a hard time keeping your mind on tasks or frequently lose things you need for your work?

Lose things? Keep my mind on tasks? No, not really. I mean, I just do my work. I don't really lose my tools or anything. I always keep my big master key ring clipped right to my belt loop. They tried giving me one of those retractable lanyard things a couple of years ago, but the spring inside it snapped after like a week. Cheap plastic. 

Speaking of those keys, we have this one supply closet down by the old boiler room, and the key for it is this massive, heavy brass thing. It seriously looks like it belongs in a medieval dungeon. I asked the locksmith who comes in—guy named Gary, real nice guy, always wears these loud Hawaiian shirts even in the dead of winter—I asked him why we couldn't just swap the core out for a normal lock. He told me the door frame is actually warped from the heat over the years, so a standard deadbolt wouldn't line up right. 

Gary's got this bulldog that rides in his work van with him, by the way. Meatball, he calls him. Ugliest dog you've ever seen, just a face full of wrinkles, but sweet as pie. He drools all over the dashboard, though. I told Gary he needs to keep a microfiber rag up there, but he just laughs it off. Microfiber is great for that kind of thing, really traps the moisture. We use them for the lobby windows... 

Wait, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, losing things. Yeah, no, I don't really lose my stuff or zone out on the job. I just can't stop moving around.
Do you often find that you act or speak without thinking, such as blurting out answers or interrupting others frequently?

Yeah, I do that a lot. Like when my supervisor or one of the church staff starts giving me instructions, I just jump right in with what I think they're going to say before they even finish. Half the time I get it wrong and they have to correct me. It's just... they talk so slow sometimes, you know? 

Like Father Thomas at the church I clean on the weekends. He's a great guy, really, but he talks like he's got all the time in the world. He'll start telling me about how the pews need extra polishing for a wedding, and I'm already halfway down the aisle with the lemon oil. I use this specific brand of lemon oil, actually. You can't just use the cheap stuff from the grocery store, it leaves a residue that attracts dust like a magnet. You need the commercial grade stuff. I get it from this janitorial supply place downtown. The guy who runs it, Sal, he's been there since the 80s. He's got this massive collection of vintage bowling balls in the back of his shop. Beautiful swirls on them, blues and greens. He says he used to be in a league with his brothers. They had matching satin jackets and everything. Satin is a nightmare to get stains out of, by the way. If you spill coffee on it, you might as well just throw it away. Though, if you catch it quick enough with some club soda...

Wait, sorry, what was the question? Oh, interrupting. Yeah, I jump in a lot. I just can't wait for them to get to the point.
Do you often find that you make careless mistakes in your work because you have trouble paying close attention to the details?

Careless mistakes? No, I don't really do that. I mean, cleaning is pretty straightforward, you know? You sweep, you mop, you wipe things down. It's not like I'm doing brain surgery or anything. I just get in there and get it done. Fast, too. I'm usually the first one finished with my section. 

The only thing is, sometimes I get moving so fast that I might knock a trash can over or something. We have these big, heavy-duty plastic bins on wheels—the gray ones, not the blue recycling ones. The wheels on those things are terrible, by the way. They squeak like crazy. I brought in some WD-40 from home to spray them, but my boss told me we're not allowed to use aerosol lubricants indoors because of some air quality regulation. So now I have to use this weird silicone grease that comes in a tube. It's so messy. Gets all over your gloves. 

I buy my own gloves, actually. The ones they provide are those cheap, thin latex ones that rip if you look at them wrong. I get the thick nitrile ones, the black ones. Makes you look like a mechanic or a tattoo artist or something. My nephew is a tattoo artist. He's got his own shop down in the arts district. He did this huge dragon piece on a guy's back that took like three days. I don't know how anyone could sit still for that long. I'd go out of my mind sitting in a chair for three days while someone pokes me with a needle. He says the shading is the hardest part...

Wait, what did you ask me? Mistakes? No, I don't really make careless mistakes. I just work fast.
